## Worked example

O011-W1 / item_version 1, worked_example. **Prompt:** Hypothetical three-month IR future: EUR500000 principal, F=100−annual rate in percent, tick0.01 quote point, agreed quarter-year fraction0.25, initial margin EUR500 per contract. A lender/depositor buys 1 at 90.50; it could close at 90.55 after 14 days or instead hold to price EDSP 91.25. Derive tick value and position direction; compute close P/L, margin return and simple365-day annualisation, held P/L, annual spot rate and effective deposit rate for matching total principal. For alternative physical placement at a rate0.05 percentage point below the benchmark, calculate separate compensation using the same0.25 fraction, add it to the actual interest and the held futures gain, and derive the final effective rate. Derive the rate adjustment from cash flows. Explain why using91/365 instead changes the result and why the illustration is not a universal discounted daily-futures hedge.

**Steps and interpretation:** Tick in rate is0.01 percentage point=.0001 annual decimal. Tick money=500000×.0001×.25=EUR12.50. Price rises when rate falls, so long hedges a lender against falling deposit rates; a borrower exposed to rising rates takes short. Close G=1×12.5×(90.55−90.50)/.01=EUR62.500000; margin return 12.5%, annualised 325.893%. Held G=EUR937.500000; spot rate=(100−91.25)/100=0.087500 annual decimal. Matching principal EUR500000, cash interest L×spot×.25; add G and divide by L×.25 gives effective rate 9.5%, the entry-implied 9.50%. Physical received rate=8.7%; compensation=L×(i_benchmark−i_received)×.25=EUR62.500000. Actual interest=L×0.087000×.25 plus compensation restores benchmark interest; adding held futures G then gives the same9.5% effective annual rate. Futures gain and placement compensation are distinct flows, not the same payment counted twice. This uses one consistent quarter-year convention and undiscounted comparison. Replacing only denominator .25 with91/365 mixes conventions and slightly changes the effective rate; explicit all-leg day-count/timing treatment is needed. The note records unreconciled source discounted/non-discounted expressions, so no universal exact daily-settled hedge or margin-account value is claimed. Close and held paths are alternative outcomes.

source_units.heading: Rubric and independence
source_units.text:
## Rubric and independence

Pass requires every listed component, all requested outputs and essential keyed reasoning without a critical conceptual error. Algebraically equivalent formulas, explicitly defined opposite cash-flow signs and equivalent plain-language reasoning are accepted. Partial means a missing component or a correct method with an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail means the central mechanism or condition is wrong. Unscorable means the response or help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown conditions never certify independence. Arithmetic slips require independent correction before a pass. No numerical grade is invented.

Critical errors: Treating quote tick as0.01 annual decimal; short for a lender against falling rates; adding money directly to a rate; mixing fractions; universalising unreconciled source expressions.

Acquisition requires two distinct unassisted passes from I1/I2/D1/D2 using the exact six routes in metadata. Each full prompt and key covers every component; any pair therefore covers the whole outcome twice. A fresh D item used for acquisition cannot later certify delayed retention. Worked/support/prerequisite items and the narrow C1 correction cannot substitute for a full check. The finite bank must not be reused after exposure; request a plan_issue when fewer than two fresh full items remain.

## Misconceptions and correction

A correct gain with a wrong effective rate often arises from an inconsistent accrual denominator. State each rate in annual decimal and each time fraction before adding money to interest. source_units.heading: Motivation and explanation
source_units.text:
## Motivation and explanation

Bond quotes are prices per100 face. A100000-face contract therefore multiplies each quote point by1000. Clean price omits accrued coupon; full price adds it. A conversion factor prices the deliverable at the contract reference yield, rather than its market yield: PV the remaining coupons and principal at the later coupon date, add the coupon due at that date and discount the combined cash value back to the earlier valuation date using the declared fraction, subtract reference accrued coupon, divide by100. The finished-note example uses semiannual coupon4 and periodic reference yield.035; its later-date value $P_{AN}=\sum_{j=1}^{22}\frac{4}{1.035^j}+\frac{100}{1.035^{22}}$. Earlier full value is $P_F=(P_{AN}+4)/(1.035)^{\mathrm{fraction}}$, followed by the stated accrued-coupon subtraction and /100. Its170/171 convention conflict prevents blindly copying a numerical factor. In prepared calculations CF is declared consistently. Delivery cash per100 is futures clean price×CF+delivery accrued coupon. A short carry trade borrows, buys the cash bond, receives/reinvests coupons, delivers and repays. Simplified daily carry = annual coupon/365−full purchase price×funding rate/365. Positive constant carry rewards later delivery, negative earlier, only under the note's simplified conditions. CF corrects reference characteristics, not actual funding economics; CTD needs eligible-basket comparison.

## Complete checked-note explanation

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; the earlier concise teaching prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisite lessons remain the routes specified above. Course-organization details in O001 are supporting context, not additional scoring components.

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/Bond_Futures_Conversion_Factors_and_Delivery.md#Bond futures, conversion factors and delivery]]; fingerprint `a9656034a515703d258f470320f1ea171d1dcd964701cf8a1f19c755171cfec1`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Bond futures, conversion factors and delivery

How can one futures contract allow delivery of several real bonds when its underlying asset is a notional bond? Long-term bond futures specify a standardized reference instrument, then use a **conversion factor** to adjust the invoice for an eligible deliverable bond. The short chooses the bond and, in this tutorial, its delivery date within the month. Those options connect bond pricing to financing and coupon income. The lecture's hypothetical terms are recorded as supplied examples. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 2]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 9]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 13]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]]

#### The notional contract and its monetary scale

The **Long-term Treasury Bond Futures Tutorial** refers to a notional 20-year Treasury bond with USD 100,000 face value and 7% yield to maturity. Its quotation $QP$ is a clean price per USD 100 nominal value, excluding accrued coupon. Since $100000/100=1000$,

$$CV=1000\,QP,$$

where $CV$ is contract value in dollars. A tick is USD 0.01 in the quoted price, so it changes contract value by $1000(0.01)=\text{USD }10$. Initial margin is USD 2,000, 2% of nominal contract value. Delivery months are March, June, September and December. The last trading day is two business days before the last business day of the delivery month. The short can deliver on any business day of the month. The source defines EDSP as the contract's futures price at 11:00 a.m. on the second business day before that last trading date. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 9]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/assets/Week_2_L11_Bond_Specification.png]]

*The full hypothetical specification distinguishes the quotation per USD 100 from the USD 100,000 contract. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 9]]*

The source says the zero-basis-at-maturity rule is theoretically applicable to the CTD bond because the underlying reference bond is notional. This qualification links convergence to the eligible delivery choice rather than asserting that every bond's raw clean spot quotation equals the unadjusted futures quotation. The lecture does not derive a precise conversion-adjusted basis formula here. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 9]]

##### A short closing trade

The short sells ten contracts at $F_0=91.38$ and buys them back 45 days later at $F_{45}=91.23$. The quotation fell by 15 ticks. A short benefits from that fall:

$$\Pi=10(15)(10)=\text{USD }1{,}500.$$

The initial-margin return is $1500/(10\times2000)=7.5\%$. The source's simple annual scaling is $0.075\times365/45=60.83\%$. This closes the obligation before the separate delivery illustration. [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/Stock_Index_and_Currency_Futures.md#Read the contract before calculating|Read the contract before calculating]] explains the common sign and margin-denominator rules. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10]]

#### Clean price, full price and coupon dates

A clean price excludes accrued coupon. A **full price** includes the compensation owed to the seller for coupon accrued since the previous coupon payment:

$$P_{\mathrm{full}}=P_{\mathrm{clean}}+AC.$$

All quantities must use the same face-value basis. A purchase of the source's eligible bond costs a full spot price, while the contract quotes clean. This distinction is necessary when comparing the initial cash outflow with the eventual delivery invoice. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 9]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

The eligible-bond example has USD 100 face value, an annual coupon of 8% paid semi-annually, hence USD 4 per coupon, and 12 years remaining from the previous coupon date. The timeline records a previous coupon on 18 November, purchase today on 1 April, the next coupon on 18 May, and the after-next coupon on 18 November. It displays a June delivery month, initial full spot price $S_0=99.13$, initial clean futures quotation $F_0=88.19$, and financing rate $r=6\%$. These values belong to the delivery example, not the earlier $91.38\to91.23$ closing trade. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/assets/Week_2_L11_Bond_Delivery_Timeline.png]]

*The original delivery timeline keeps coupon dates, full spot price and clean futures quotation visible. Its displayed day counts are source assumptions; related inconsistencies are discussed below. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10]]*

#### Conversion factor: price at the contract's reference yield

A bond's conversion factor $CF$ is its **clean price per one unit of face value when valued at the contract's 7% reference yield**. It is dimensionless. The exchange calculates a factor for the first day of each delivery month and keeps that factor constant during the delivery cycle, using its specified rounding conventions. The source's adjusted clean delivery price is

$$P_{\mathrm{delivery,clean}}=CF\times FP,$$

where $FP$ is the contract's futures quotation. Accrued coupon must then be added to obtain the full invoice price. A factor above one increases the clean invoice relative to $FP$; a factor below one reduces it. In the source's valuation example, a coupon above the 7% reference yield gives $CF>1$, and one below it gives $CF<1$. This is a reference-yield adjustment, rather than a claim that different eligible bonds have identical current market prices or implied repo rates. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

##### Follow the source's valuation steps

The coupon is USD 4 every half year and the reference half-year yield is $0.07/2=0.035$. On the after-next coupon date, the source values 22 remaining coupon payments and the final principal:

$$P_{AN}=\sum_{t=1}^{22}\frac{4}{(1.035)^t}+\frac{100}{(1.035)^{22}}
\approx107.584.$$

Here $t$ counts half-year periods. Each payment is discounted to that coupon date. To obtain the full price at the beginning of June, the source adds the USD 4 coupon due at the later valuation date, then discounts back a fractional half-year. Its printed formula is

$$P_F=\frac{107.584+4}{(1.035)^{171/182.5}}=108.065\quad\text{(source's displayed equality)}.$$

It subtracts accrued coupon for 14 days to obtain a clean price:

$$P_C=108.065-\frac{14}{182.5}(4)=107.758,$$

and divides by 100 face value to give $CF=1.07758$. The cash-flow reasoning is: discount future full value, remove accrued coupon, normalize by face value. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11]]

##### The conversion-factor example has a day-count error

The printed formula's **171** days disagree with the **170** days on the source timeline and with its numerical result. Evaluating the printed expression gives approximately $108.044$ for $P_F$, $107.737$ for the clean price, and $CF\approx1.077373$. Using **170/182.5** gives $108.065$, $107.758$ and $1.07758$, matching the displayed results. These are agent recomputations from the original source formula and data. The note preserves both the printed formula and its discrepancy, rather than treating the stated factor as a verified consequence of 171 days. Use an explicitly supplied consistent factor for later calculations, or state a consistent day-count choice. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/assets/Week_2_L11_Conversion_Factor_Example.png]]

*Source conversion-factor definition, coupon timeline and printed calculations. The 171-day exponent and 170-day diagram are both visible. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11]]*

#### The short's cost-of-carry transaction

The short borrows in the money market, uses the loan to pay the full bond purchase price, and acquires the bond. During the holding period, the bond produces coupon income while the loan produces a financing cost. At delivery, the short transfers the bond to the long, receives the invoice price, and repays the loan. The source calls

$$\mathrm{carry}=\mathrm{carry\ revenue}-\mathrm{carry\ expenditure}.$$

It uses accrued coupon as carry revenue and interest on the financed full purchase price as carry expenditure. This sign convention matters: positive carry means that continuing to hold the financed bond earns more than it costs. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 12]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/assets/Week_2_L11_Cost_of_Carry_Flows.png]]

*The six labeled flows show borrowing, bond acquisition, delivery, payment and loan repayment. The diagram links cash financing to the physical delivery obligation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 12]]*

#### Delivery timing under the source's carry rule

The source's rule chooses the last business day of the delivery month when daily carry is positive, and the first business day when it is negative. Its example computes, per USD 100 face value,

$$\mathrm{daily\ revenue}=\frac{0.08(100)}{365}=0.02192,$$

$$\mathrm{daily\ financing\ cost}=\frac{99.13(0.06)}{365}=0.01630,$$

so daily carry is approximately USD 0.00562. Continuing to hold adds positive carry, giving the source's choice of the last business day. With negative carry, waiting instead erodes the transaction's return. This is the lecture's simplified constant daily-carry rule. Its stronger sentence that in reality only the first or last business day is chosen is retained as a source assertion, not expanded into a universal market rule beyond the illustration. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 13]]

#### What to carry forward

The contract quotation, full bond purchase price and full invoice price have different roles. Conversion factors adjust the clean delivery amount for a chosen bond, while accrued coupon completes the invoice. Carry links the bond's income to the financing cost and determines the source's delivery-date choice. [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/Implied_Repo_Rate_and_Cheapest_to_Deliver.md|Implied repo rate and cheapest to deliver]] develops the next question: which eligible bond gives the greatest return from purchase to delivery? [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 12]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 13]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]]

source_units.heading: Rubric and independence
source_units.text:
## Rubric and independence

Pass requires every listed component, all requested outputs and essential keyed reasoning without a critical conceptual error. Algebraically equivalent formulas, explicitly defined opposite cash-flow signs and equivalent plain-language reasoning are accepted. Partial means a missing component or a correct method with an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail means the central mechanism or condition is wrong. Unscorable means the response or help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown conditions never certify independence. Arithmetic slips require independent correction before a pass. No numerical grade is invented.

Critical errors: Applying accrued coupon before multiplying CF; calling CF a market price or funding rate; dimensional missing face multiplier; universal first/last date assertion; choosing CTD from lowest clean price.

Acquisition requires two distinct unassisted passes from I1/I2/D1/D2 using the exact six routes in metadata. Each full prompt and key covers every component; any pair therefore covers the whole outcome twice. A fresh D item used for acquisition cannot later certify delayed retention. Worked/support/prerequisite items and the narrow C1 correction cannot substitute for a full check. The finite bank must not be reused after exposure; request a plan_issue when fewer than two fresh full items remain.

| Component | I1 | I2 | D1 | D2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| bond_quote_payoff_and_margin | required | required | required | required |
| reference_valuation_and_invoice | required | required | required | required |
| carry_timing_and_selection_limits | required | required | required | required |

## Misconceptions and correction

Confusing clean and full invoice loses a coupon component. Keep two labelled columns: clean FP×CF, then delivery AC. Distinguish reference yield from market/funding yield. Observe the learner's reasoning before diagnosing: a sign or omitted word alone is tentative. Score before help. O012-C1 / item_version 1, narrow_correction. **Fresh prompt:** Fresh narrow check: futures clean quote80, CF1.10, delivery AC2 per100. Full invoice is (80+2)×1.10? **Key and rubric:** No:80×1.10+2=90 per100. Factor scales clean reference price, while actual accrued coupon is added after. Pass only if the keyed repaired component is supplied; partial for an omission or arithmetic slip; fail for the same conflicting mechanism. C1 is not a full independent check. After two ineffective hints show the relevant worked step; after another failed correction pause and return to the named prerequisite or explanation.

source_units.heading: Outcome and conditions
source_units.text:
## Outcome and conditions

Derive one-coupon and no-coupon implied repo returns and rank a given eligible basket under explicit conventions. Required components: full_cashflow_identity_and_formula, numeric_rates_and_eligible_ranking, financing_and_source_limits. Supported work may use the cited notes; independent checks use no notes, internet, solution or hints. 1. Read **Motivation and explanation** for the decision, definitions and conditions before performing calculations.

source_units.heading: Motivation and explanation
source_units.text:
## Motivation and explanation

A short-financed delivery resembles a loan: buy the full cash bond PP at time0 and receive full invoice IP at delivery. With simple annual r and n days, the initial cash grows to $PP(1+rn/365)$. If coupon C is received m days before delivery and reinvested at this same r, receipts are $IP+C(1+rm/365)$. Equating sides, collect r terms: $r(PP n-Cm)/365=IP+C-PP$. A nonzero denominator therefore gives $r=365(IP+C-PP)/(PP n-Cm)$. No coupon sets C=0, yielding $365(IP-PP)/(PP n)$. These are implied annual repo returns under the stated model, not a compounded project IRR. The finished-note source's printed3.57% does not exactly match its given inputs: using43/180 accrued coupon yields about3.61742%; the note exposes the mismatch. Prepared examples specify consistent full inputs, coupon dates and365 convention. CTD maximises comparable eligible IRR; actual borrowing costs, fees and cash-flow timing decide realised profit. No actual basket in notes means no actual CTD can be named.

source_units.text:
## Complete checked-note explanation

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; the earlier concise teaching prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisite lessons remain the routes specified above. Course-organization details in O001 are supporting context, not additional scoring components.

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/Implied_Repo_Rate_and_Cheapest_to_Deliver.md#Implied repo rate and cheapest to deliver]]; fingerprint `cc1472840d045ac50e647cb4be41302f7eeca6bf21ea19e86c7d6305b27d2153`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Implied repo rate and cheapest to deliver

Which bond should a short select when several bonds are eligible for delivery into the same futures contract? The lecture identifies the **cheapest-to-deliver (CTD)** bond as the eligible bond with the highest **implied repo rate (IRR)**. IRR measures the annualized return implied by buying a bond at its full spot price and realizing the delivery invoice and any intervening coupon. Here IRR means implied repo rate throughout; it does not refer to a generic project internal rate of return. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

[[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/Bond_Futures_Conversion_Factors_and_Delivery.md|Bond futures, conversion factors and delivery]] explains the conversion-factor and accrued-coupon inputs. Selecting the lowest unadjusted clean market price would ignore the different delivery proceeds and coupon cash flows. The CTD comparison must consider the complete transaction on a consistent day-count and quotation basis. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

#### Why the return resembles a repo loan

The source compares an actual repo, in which cash is advanced against a bond and returned with interest, with a purchase-to-futures-delivery transaction. Buying the bond creates an initial cash outflow. Delivering the bond into the futures contract creates a later cash inflow. These flows can be described as an **implied loan**: the purchase amount is the advance and the delivery proceeds are its repayment. The bond may also pay a coupon before delivery, which the source assumes can be reinvested at the same implied rate until delivery. The short's actual money-market borrowing is a separate financing leg. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]]

The initial outflow includes the clean market price and accrued coupon paid to the bond seller. The terminal inflow includes the conversion-adjusted clean futures price and accrued coupon paid by the receiver at delivery. If a coupon arrives before delivery, its reinvested amount also contributes to the terminal value. Thus IRR compares a complete stream of purchase and delivery cash flows, rather than comparing the futures quotation directly with the clean market price. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

#### Notation, units and assumptions

Use all prices on the same face-value basis, such as dollars per USD 100 face value. Define:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $PP$ | Full purchasing price today |
| $MP$ | Clean market purchasing price today |
| $IP$ | Full invoice price at delivery |
| $FP$ | Contract's clean futures quotation |
| $CF$ | Deliverable bond's dimensionless conversion factor |
| $C$ | One periodic coupon payment |
| $n_{T,DL}$ | Days from today ($T$) to delivery ($DL$) |
| $n_{NC,DL}$ | Days from the next coupon ($NC$) to delivery |
| $AC_{PC,T}$ | Coupon accrued from previous coupon ($PC$) to today |
| $AC_{NC,DL}$ | Coupon accrued from next coupon to delivery |
| $AC_{PC,DL}$ | Coupon accrued from previous coupon to delivery |
| $AC_{T,DL}$ | Coupon accrued from today to delivery when no coupon intervenes |

The source formulas use simple annual rate accrual with day fractions $n/365$. In the one-coupon case, they assume that coupon is reinvested at IRR. There are no fees or taxes in the displayed cash-flow equations. IRR is an implied transaction yield. Compare it with actual financing separately when discussing whether the financed transaction is profitable. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

#### One coupon before delivery

The purchase is $PP=MP+AC_{PC,T}$. After the intervening coupon, accrued coupon restarts, so the delivery invoice is

$$IP=FP\,CF+AC_{NC,DL}.$$

The purchase amount accumulated to delivery must equal the invoice plus the coupon accumulated from its own payment date:

$$PP\left(1+IRR\frac{n_{T,DL}}{365}\right)
=IP+C\left(1+IRR\frac{n_{NC,DL}}{365}\right).$$

The right-hand coupon interest covers fewer days because the coupon arrives after the bond purchase. Expanding and collecting the $IRR$ terms gives

$$\frac{IRR}{365}\left(PP\,n_{T,DL}-C\,n_{NC,DL}\right)=IP+C-PP,$$

and therefore

$$\boxed{IRR=\frac{(IP+C-PP)365}{PP\,n_{T,DL}-C\,n_{NC,DL}}}.$$

The numerator is the undiscounted surplus, scaled to an annual rate. The denominator accounts for the amount and duration of invested cash, reduced by the coupon that arrives before delivery and can be reinvested. Both numerator and denominator use money times days, so the ratio is a dimensionless annual rate. The algebra requires a nonzero denominator. These intermediate steps are agent explanation of the source's displayed cash-flow identity, not extra empirical evidence. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

##### Recompute the source's numerical example

The slide gives $PP=99.13$, $FP=88.19$, $CF=1.07758$, coupon $C=4$, $n_{T,DL}=89$ and $n_{NC,DL}=43$. The source's printed accrued coupon is $4(43/180)$. Substituting its numbers literally gives

$$IRR=\frac{\left(88.19(1.07758)+4\frac{43}{180}+4-99.13\right)365}
{99.13(89)-4(43)}
\approx0.0361742=3.61742\%.$$

**The slide reports 3.57%, which does not follow from those printed inputs.** Using $43/182.5$ instead gives about 3.56219%, close to its reported figure but still not identical. The preceding conversion-factor example also mixes a 170-day timeline with a 171-day exponent. These are source arithmetic/day-count inconsistencies. The generic cash-flow equation and its algebra are usable; the stated numerical example must not be taught as an exact verified answer. An exercise should give a consistent coupon day count and either a verified or explicitly assumed conversion factor. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

The diagram labels intervals of 46, 14 and 29 days, whereas the numerical formula uses 89 days from today to delivery and 43 days from the next coupon to delivery. Its printed calendar dates and displayed intervals should therefore be treated as the source's example conventions, rather than silently recalculated into a new calendar interpretation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/assets/Week_2_L11_IRR_Formulas.png]]

*The source includes both IRR cases, the complete notation and the numerical expression. Its 3.57% label and mixed day-count inputs remain visible for checking. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]*

#### No coupon before delivery

Without an intervening coupon, the accumulated purchase amount equals the invoice:

$$PP\left(1+IRR\frac{n_{T,DL}}{365}\right)=IP,$$

where the invoice uses coupon accrued since the last payment,

$$IP=FP\,CF+AC_{PC,DL}.$$

Subtracting $PP$ and dividing by the initial amount and time fraction gives

$$\boxed{IRR=\frac{(IP-PP)365}{PP\,n_{T,DL}}}.$$

The distinction from the one-coupon formula follows from the cash flows: there is no coupon to reinvest, so no $C$ term enters the numerator or denominator. In the source's no-coupon setting, the short pays $AC_{PC,T}$ at purchase but receives $AC_{PC,DL}$ at delivery. The net accrued coupon is $AC_{T,DL}$, provided the same coupon-accrual convention applies across the whole interval. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

#### Compare eligible bonds and choose CTD

For each eligible bond, determine the full purchase price, its conversion factor, the delivery invoice, coupon cash flows and applicable dates. Calculate IRR using the case that matches those cash flows. The source defines CTD as the eligible bond with **maximum IRR**, and says exchanges calculate and publish IRRs. This does not mean the highest-coupon bond or the lowest quoted-price bond must be CTD. The invoice adjustment and acquisition cost matter jointly. The uploaded lecture supplies one worked bond, rather than a table of several candidates, so no actual CTD security is identified here. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

The source's carrying illustration finances at 6%. Using its literal numerical IRR inputs gives an implied yield around 3.62%, below that financing rate. This comparison is an agent inference from the supplied figures: a positive IRR alone does not establish a positive financed profit. CTD remains a comparison among the eligible delivery alternatives. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

#### What to carry forward

Start with the full purchase outflow and finish with the full invoice plus any intervening coupon. The reinvestment assumption determines the one-coupon denominator. The CTD criterion is the greatest implied transaction yield among eligible bonds under comparable conventions. Reliable practice can use the source's formulas and explicit assumptions; exact reproduction of its inconsistent example requires clarification. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_2/L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx|L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15]]

source_units.heading: Rubric and independence
source_units.text:
## Rubric and independence

Pass requires every listed component, all requested outputs and essential keyed reasoning without a critical conceptual error. Algebraically equivalent formulas, explicitly defined opposite cash-flow signs and equivalent plain-language reasoning are accepted. Partial means a missing component or a correct method with an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail means the central mechanism or condition is wrong. Unscorable means the response or help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown conditions never certify independence. Arithmetic slips require independent correction before a pass. No numerical grade is invented.

Critical errors: Ignoring coupon reinvestment or accrued coupon; inconsistent day count; lowest clean price criterion; positive implied return asserted as profit irrespective of financing.

Acquisition requires two distinct unassisted passes from I1/I2/D1/D2 using the exact six routes in metadata. Each full prompt and key covers every component; any pair therefore covers the whole outcome twice. A fresh D item used for acquisition cannot later certify delayed retention. Worked/support/prerequisite items and the narrow C1 correction cannot substitute for a full check. The finite bank must not be reused after exposure; request a plan_issue when fewer than two fresh full items remain.

| Component | I1 | I2 | D1 | D2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| full_cashflow_identity_and_formula | required | required | required | required |
| numeric_rates_and_eligible_ranking | required | required | required | required |
| financing_and_source_limits | required | required | required | required |

## Misconceptions and correction

A positive yield is a return before its funding leg. Write the repayment identity first and keep the actual repo rate separate; a purchase price comparison alone loses coupons and the delivery factor. Observe the learner's reasoning before diagnosing: a sign or omitted word alone is tentative. Score before help. O013-C1 / item_version 1, narrow_correction. **Fresh prompt:** Fresh narrow check: no coupon, full PP100, IP101 in100 days. Does annual implied3.65% guarantee gain when funding5%? **Key and rubric:** r=(101−100)365/(100×100)=.0365. No: same simple borrowing repayment is100(1+.05×100/365)=101.369863, larger than invoice101 before fees. Pass only if the keyed repaired component is supplied; partial for an omission or arithmetic slip; fail for the same conflicting mechanism. C1 is not a full independent check. After two ineffective hints show the relevant worked step; after another failed correction pause and return to the named prerequisite or explanation.

## Motivation, intuition, and definitions

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

Origin: reused complete note introduction before the first subsection, [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Cost_of_Carry_and_Calendar_Spreads.md#Cost of carry and calendar spreads]], fingerprint `7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d`.

### Cost of carry and calendar spreads

What determines a fair delivery price when an asset can be bought today, financed, and held until delivery? The lecture answers by constructing two ways to obtain the same asset at the same date. Comparing their cash flows removes the need to predict the future spot price. This is the core of Week 3 because currency, bond and index pricing are applications of the same replication logic. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–5]]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 Q[Fair delivery price] --> A[Spot purchase and financing]
 Q --> B[Forward or futures delivery]
 A --> C[Income minus holding costs]
 B --> D[Match asset and delivery date]
 C --> E[No arbitrage cash flow equality]
 D --> E
 E --> F[Spot futures basis]
 E --> G[Two maturity spread]
 E --> H[Currency bond and index applications]
 E --> I[Qualifications: timing and tradability]
```

This source-grounded map follows physical slides 2–10; the present note develops slides 2–5, with the applications in the other Week 3 notes. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–10]]

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Cost_of_Carry_and_Calendar_Spreads.md#Foundations and conventions]]; fingerprint `7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Foundations and conventions

$S_0$ is today's spot price per unit of the underlying, $F_0$ today's agreed delivery price per unit, and $T$ the time to maturity in **years**. Annual decimal rates $d$ and $r$ represent respectively income/benefits and holding costs. The source lists coupons, dividends and convenience yield under $d$, and interest, insurance, storage and deterioration under $r$. In the linear model, income is $dS_0T$, cost is $rS_0T$, and **net carry** is $S_0(d-r)T$. No particular calendar day-count basis is supplied. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–4]]

A long commits to buy and a short to sell. The foundational distinction is between paying for an asset now and agreeing a delivery price now: entering the idealized forward/futures position has zero opening value, whereas acquiring the asset costs $S_0$. A financed spot position can nevertheless have zero **net** opening investment because the loan receipt pays for the purchase. No-arbitrage rules out a feasible zero-investment package with a sure positive payoff; if both the package and its reverse can be traded, its riskless payoff must be zero. These are model conditions, not a promise that any real investment earns a guaranteed return. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–4]]


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Cost_of_Carry_and_Calendar_Spreads.md#Borrow cash, buy spot and sell futures]]; fingerprint `7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Borrow cash, buy spot and sell futures

At time zero borrow $S_0$, pay it to buy one unit, and short one matching futures contract. Opening cash is $+S_0-S_0+0=0$. At maturity the asset is delivered for $F_0$, the loan principal $S_0$ and its interest $rS_0T$ are repaid, and the asset's income $dS_0T$ is received. Under the source's deterministic simple-rate/timing assumptions,

$$\Pi_{\rm cash}=F_0+dS_0T-S_0-rS_0T.$$

Setting this to zero and collecting $S_0$ terms gives

$$F_0=S_0+S_0(r-d)T=S_0[1+(r-d)T].$$

Financing raises the delivery price; income received while holding the asset lowers the net cost of replicating delivery. If quoted $F_0$ exceeds this value, the package earns a sure positive modeled payoff: buy the asset cheaply through spot plus financing and sell the expensive delivery commitment. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/assets/Week_3_L12_Cash_Strategy.png]]

Source slide 3: opening loan/purchase cancel, and maturity inflows equal maturity outflows at the fair price. The asset's uncertain resale price does not enter because the asset is delivered under the agreed contract. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3]]


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Cost_of_Carry_and_Calendar_Spreads.md#Borrow the asset, sell spot and buy futures]]; fingerprint `7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Borrow the asset, sell spot and buy futures

For the reverse strategy, borrow the asset, sell it for $S_0$, invest the proceeds and open a long matching futures position. Opening net cash is again zero. At maturity the deposit returns $S_0+rS_0T$. Pay $F_0$ to take delivery, return the asset to its owner and compensate the owner for income $dS_0T$. Thus

$$\Pi_{\rm reverse}=S_0+rS_0T-F_0-dS_0T.$$

This is the negative of the first payoff. If $F_0$ is too low, buy delivery cheaply and sell the asset now. When both strategies are feasible, neither sign can generate a riskless gain, forcing the equality above. In this strategy $r$ is the modeled deposit return, whereas slide 3 uses it as financing cost; the common rate and reversible cash flows are substantive assumptions. Shorting restrictions or different borrowing/lending terms can replace one exact price by a range. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 4]]


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Cost_of_Carry_and_Calendar_Spreads.md#Basis, carry, contango and backwardation]]; fingerprint `7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Basis, carry, contango and backwardation

The course defines basis as **spot minus futures**, $B_0=S_0-F_0$. Therefore

$$B_0=S_0(d-r)T.$$

If $d>r$, net carry and basis are positive, so $F_0<S_0$: the lecture calls this backwardation. If $d<r$, carry and basis are negative, so $F_0>S_0$: contango. If $d=r$, $F_0=S_0$. These price relations follow from the stated model and sign convention. A positive **cost** of carry $r-d$ has the opposite sign to positive **net** carry $d-r$; interchanging the terms reverses the conclusion. No forecast of future spot prices follows solely from these inequalities. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3–4]]


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Cost_of_Carry_and_Calendar_Spreads.md#What makes the replication valid]]; fingerprint `7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### What makes the replication valid

The lecture's linear rates, known income/costs, tradeable underlying, available short sales, matching delivery and locked funding underpin the derivation. A convenience benefit from physical ownership need not be a cash coupon transferable to a short seller. Thus listing convenience yield on slide 2 does not establish that every asset supports both exact arbitrages. **External qualification:** Damodaran's NYU “Futures Arbitrage,” sections “Storable Commodities” and “Stock Index Futures,” explains that funding differences, shorting costs and uncertain dividends weaken exact replication. These are reasons to inspect feasibility before applying the equation. [Damodaran, consulted sections](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/invfables/futurearb.htm). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–5]]

The source aggregates all futures flows at delivery. Actual futures have daily variation margin, as explained in the Week 1 margin note. That cash timing, funding and reinvestment can matter; this note preserves the lecture's simplified replication rather than treating a forward-style cash-flow table as a complete margin-funding model. The simple formula also differs from compounded conventions: do not replace it silently by an exponential. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3–5]]

source_units.text:
## Worked example

O014-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. **Prompt:** One unit of a hypothetical storable asset costs $S_0=100$ currency units. Annual simple holding/funding cost is $r=0.06$ and known transferable income yield $d=0.02$; delivery is in $T=0.5$ years. Assume reversible borrowing/lending/shorting, equal relevant rates, matching asset/delivery, deterministic cash income, and aggregate terminal futures flows. Construct both zero-net-opening-investment strategies with every terminal flow; derive and calculate fair $F_0$ and spot-minus-futures basis. Explain contango/backwardation and what it says about a future-spot forecast. Evaluate delivery quotes $103.500000$ and $100.500000$ and give the feasible arbitrage direction and profit per unit for each. Finally identify why convenience benefits, shorting/funding restrictions or daily margin could invalidate the exact equality.

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** Borrow $100$, buy one unit and short the delivery commitment: opening $+100-100=0$, terminal $F_0+dS_0T-S_0-rS_0T$. Reverse: borrow/sell one unit, invest $100$ and go long; terminal $S_0+rS_0T-F_0-dS_0T$. The payoffs are negatives under the stated identical reversible terms. Zeroing either gives $F_0=S_0[1+(r-d)T]=102.000000$ and $B_0=S_0-F_0=-2.000000$. The futures price exceeds spot, so this is contango. These are current model price relations, not a forecast of terminal spot. At the high quote, borrow cash/buy spot/short delivery; profit is $103.500000+0.02(100)(0.5)-100-0.06(100)(0.5)=1.500000$. At the low quote, borrow asset/sell spot/invest/go long; profit is $100+0.06(100)(0.5)-100.500000-0.02(100)(0.5)=1.500000$. A nontransferable convenience benefit is not necessarily cash that a short can compensate, and asymmetric funding or shorting restrictions can prevent reversing the package. Daily variation-margin dates create funding/reinvestment effects omitted by this terminal model; exact equality is conditional, not universal. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

## Misconceptions and correction

An observed omitted term/sign is tentative until the learner explains it; compare the reasoning with the critical errors above. Score the original response before providing help. Route a conceptual failure to the relevant included derivation and prerequisite, then use an unused full form.

O014-C1, item_version 1, narrow_correction. **Prompt:** A cash-flow derivation has replaced an uncertain terminal price by its expectation and then calls its realized payoff guaranteed. Is the inference justified, and what must a riskless replication establish instead? **Key/rubric:** No: an expectation is not a realized amount. Matching feasible dated inflows/outflows must cancel uncertain states or contract the necessary conversions. Pass requires the distinction and matching condition; partial for missing one, fail for equating expectation with certainty. This repairs a common inference only; it cannot substitute for a full numerical/capability check.

Give at most two hints (first identify the date/unit, second point to the included identity); after ineffective hints show the relevant worked step. After two unsuccessful independent attempts stop repeated quizzing, revisit the explanation/prerequisite and preserve the unresolved status.

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** Borrow $120$, buy one unit and short the delivery commitment: opening $+120-120=0$, terminal $F_0+dS_0T-S_0-rS_0T$. source_units.heading: Motivation, intuition, and definitions
source_units.text:
## Motivation, intuition, and definitions

Build a three-date funded calendar package and derive the earlier-minus-later spread using the intervening holding interval and earlier delivery price. The central question is which dated cash flows cancel and which risk remains. Match quantities and dates before simplifying an equation. The complete reused passages establish every academic claim, notation choice and qualification assessed here; necessary prerequisites use the complete lessons above.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Cost_of_Carry_and_Calendar_Spreads.md#Carry between two delivery dates]]; fingerprint `7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Carry between two delivery dates

Let $F_0^1,F_0^2$ be current prices for deliveries at $T^1<T^2$, both measured in years, and put $\Delta T=T^2-T^1$. Today go long the earlier contract, short the later one, and arrange a forward loan for the interval $[T^1,T^2]$. The source assigns zero initial cash to each agreement. At $T^1$ draw $F_0^1$ under the arranged loan and pay the earlier contract to acquire the asset. Hold it only for $\Delta T$; the source measures income and financing cost relative to the amount $F_0^1$ financed. At $T^2$ deliver for $F_0^2$ and repay the loan:

$$0=[F_0^2+dF_0^1\Delta T]-[F_0^1+rF_0^1\Delta T].$$

Moving the delivery-price terms to one side gives

$$F_0^1-F_0^2=F_0^1(d-r)(T^2-T^1),\qquad F_0^2=F_0^1[1+(r-d)\Delta T].$$

The earlier-minus-later spread equals carry over the **intervening** interval. Using $T^2$ instead of $T^2-T^1$ would charge for time before the asset was acquired. Using $S_0$ rather than $F_0^1$ would change the financing base in the source's construction. This is a separate interval model with funding terms locked today, not a license to combine inconsistent rates across maturities. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 5]]


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Cost_of_Carry_and_Calendar_Spreads.md#What makes the replication valid]]; fingerprint `7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### What makes the replication valid

The lecture's linear rates, known income/costs, tradeable underlying, available short sales, matching delivery and locked funding underpin the derivation. A convenience benefit from physical ownership need not be a cash coupon transferable to a short seller. Thus listing convenience yield on slide 2 does not establish that every asset supports both exact arbitrages. **External qualification:** Damodaran's NYU “Futures Arbitrage,” sections “Storable Commodities” and “Stock Index Futures,” explains that funding differences, shorting costs and uncertain dividends weaken exact replication. These are reasons to inspect feasibility before applying the equation. [Damodaran, consulted sections](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/invfables/futurearb.htm). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–5]]

The source aggregates all futures flows at delivery. Actual futures have daily variation margin, as explained in the Week 1 margin note. That cash timing, funding and reinvestment can matter; this note preserves the lecture's simplified replication rather than treating a forward-style cash-flow table as a complete margin-funding model. The simple formula also differs from compounded conventions: do not replace it silently by an exponential. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3–5]]

## Worked example

O015-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. **Prompt:** Two current delivery prices concern one matching asset at $T^1=0.5$ and $T^2=1$ years. The earlier quote is $F_0^1=100$. A forward loan can be locked today for the intervening interval at annual simple $r=0.06$; known holding income is $d=0.02$ on the source model base $F_0^1$. All trades are reversible and source terminal/timing assumptions hold. Draw the dated zero-investment package, derive and compute fair $F_0^2$ and earlier-minus-later spread, and interpret its sign. With later quote $103.000000$, compute package profit and its direction. Explain why $S_0$ and $T^2$ cannot replace the financing base and interval, and why this separate interval construction need not follow by mixing unrelated spot carry rates.

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** Today long earlier delivery, short later delivery and arrange a forward loan; each initial flow is zero. At $T^1$ draw $100$ and pay it for the asset. At $T^2$ receive $F_0^2+dF_0^1\Delta T$ and repay $F_0^1(1+r\Delta T)$. Thus $0=F_0^2+dF_0^1\Delta T-F_0^1-rF_0^1\Delta T$, where $\Delta T=0.5$. Hence $F_0^2=F_0^1[1+(r-d)\Delta T]=102.000000$, and $F_0^1-F_0^2=F_0^1(d-r)\Delta T=-2.000000$. The later delivery is dearer; the defined earlier-minus-later spread is negative. At the high later quote use that same long-earlier/short-later package; terminal profit is $103.000000+0.02(100)(0.5)-100-0.06(100)(0.5)=1.000000$. Its reverse changes the sign. The asset is acquired only at $T^1$ for $F_0^1$, so $S_0$ is not the loan principal and $T^2$ includes time before ownership. Funding and income must be locked and compatible for this interval. Combining different conventions or uncontracted future rates would not establish the same riskless package; margin cash timing and trading restrictions remain qualifications. source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

Origin: reused complete note introduction before the first subsection, [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Currency_Parity_and_Carry_Trade.md#Currency parity and carry trade]], fingerprint `9aaebd51a4ce2a4c8964bbf02d522f5ea81dbc1fbb36583d7990849bc3299c8d`.

### Currency parity and carry trade

How can interest rates determine a forward exchange rate, yet a currency carry trade still lose money? The distinction is whether the future conversion is contracted today or left exposed to the future spot rate. This note derives the course's covered relation before explaining its uncovered and peg-dependent examples. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6–8]]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 A[Borrow and invest in different currencies] --> B[Future conversion locked by forward]
 A --> C[Future conversion at uncertain spot]
 B --> D[Covered interest parity]
 C --> E[Uncovered parity hypothesis]
 C --> F[Carry trade gains or losses]
 E --> G[Expected exchange adjustment]
 F --> H[Funding currency appreciation risk]
 C --> I[Peg based forward example]
 I --> J[Peg survival is an assumption]
```

The map follows slides 6–8; the prerequisite is matching assets, dates and cash flows in the general carry model. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6–8]]

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Currency_Parity_and_Carry_Trade.md#Covered interest parity with dollars per euro]]; fingerprint `9aaebd51a4ce2a4c8964bbf02d522f5ea81dbc1fbb36583d7990849bc3299c8d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Covered interest parity with dollars per euro

On slide 6, $S_0$ and $F_0$ mean **dollars per euro**. Let $r_\$,r_€$ be annual simple dollar/euro rates and $\tau=T/12$ years when the slide's $T$ is in months. Borrow one euro, sell it for $S_0$ dollars and deposit those dollars. At maturity the deposit pays $S_0(1+r_\$\tau)$ dollars. The euro debt is $1+r_€\tau$ euros; arrange a forward purchase of that euro amount, equivalently a forward sale of the corresponding dollar deposit proceeds at parity. The locked dollar repayment cost is $F_0(1+r_€\tau)$. Setting the zero-investment package's dollar payoff to zero gives

$$S_0(1+r_\$\tau)=F_0(1+r_€\tau),\qquad
F_0=S_0\frac{1+r_\$\tau}{1+r_€\tau}.$$

The numerator/denominator follow the quotation: dollar investment grows at the dollar rate, but each euro owed costs $F_0$ dollars. No uncertain future spot conversion remains in this covered package. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6]]

Dividing by $S_0$ and subtracting from one yields the slide's exact relation

$$\frac{S_0-F_0}{S_0}=\frac{(r_€-r_\$)\tau}{1+r_€\tau}\approx(r_€-r_\$)\tau.$$

The approximation ignores the denominator's deviation from one; it is not an exact annualized percentage. If $r_€>r_\$$, $F_0<S_0$: one euro buys fewer dollars forward, a euro forward discount/dollar premium. If $r_€<r_\$$ the euro is at a premium. Reversing the currency quotation requires rederiving the ratio rather than keeping its sign mechanically. Rates, value dates and borrowing/lending availability must match. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/assets/Week_3_L12_Currency_Parity.png]]

The source table shows principal and interest separately; the equations above group them into maturity balances. The slide's month-to-year conversion is essential even though other slides measure $T$ directly in years. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6]]

source_units.text:
## Worked example

O016-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. **Prompt:** The spot quote is $S_0=1.2\ \mathrm{USD/EUR}$. Annual simple rates are $r_\$=0.06$ and $r_€=0.02$; maturity is 6 months. Matching value dates, equal relevant borrowing/lending terms and covered forward trades are available. Borrow one euro and derive covered interest parity by matching every maturity currency amount. Compute fair $F_0$, the exact normalized spot-minus-forward difference and its first-order approximation. Name which currency has a premium/discount under this quotation. For a quote $1.23376238\ \mathrm{USD/EUR}$ above parity, construct the reverse covered package and compute its USD payoff per initial euro acquired. Explain why the covered conclusion is not an uncovered expected-spot forecast and why quotation/time units matter.

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** Use $\tau=6/12=0.5$ years. Borrow EUR 1, sell for USD $1.2$ and invest to $S_0(1+r_\$\tau)=1.23600000$ USD. Euro debt is $1+r_€\tau=1.01000000$ EUR; forward repayment costs $F_0(1+r_€\tau)$ USD. Equalizing gives $F_0=S_0(1+r_\$\tau)/(1+r_€\tau)=1.22376238\ \mathrm{USD/EUR}$. The exact $(S_0-F_0)/S_0=((r_€-r_\$)\tau)/(1+r_€\tau)=-0.01980198$, versus approximation $(r_€-r_\$)\tau=-0.02000000$; denominator is omitted only approximately. Euro forward premium/dollar discount because USD per EUR increases. For an overpriced euro forward, borrow USD $1.2$, buy EUR 1, invest it to EUR $1.01000000$ and sell that maturity amount forward. USD receipt minus USD debt is $F_{\mathrm{quote}}(1+r_€\tau)-S_0(1+r_\$\tau)=0.01010000$. Contracting the entire conversion removes future-spot risk under the assumptions. Replacing the forward with an expectation leaves realized spot random; no UIP forecast is proved. Inverting quotation requires rederiving numerator/denominator and premium sign; using months as years misstates accrual. Matching dates and feasible rates are required. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

source_units.heading: Motivation, intuition, and definitions
source_units.text:
## Motivation, intuition, and definitions

Derive and calculate uncovered carry payoffs, distinguish expectation from realized conversion, and evaluate the checked historical-style peg/NDF illustration with explicit risk qualifications. The central question is which dated cash flows cancel and which risk remains. Match quantities and dates before simplifying an equation. The complete reused passages establish every academic claim, notation choice and qualification assessed here; necessary prerequisites use the complete lessons above.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Currency_Parity_and_Carry_Trade.md#Uncovered parity is a condition on expectations]]; fingerprint `9aaebd51a4ce2a4c8964bbf02d522f5ea81dbc1fbb36583d7990849bc3299c8d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Uncovered parity is a condition on expectations

Slide 7 replaces $F_0$ by $E_0[S_T]$ (the source writes $E_T(S)$ for the anticipated maturity spot rate) in the dollar-per-euro relation:

$$\frac{S_0-E_0[S_T]}{S_0}=\frac{(r_€-r_\$)\tau}{1+r_€\tau}.$$

Without a forward contract the actual $S_T$ remains unknown. This equation is an **uncovered interest parity hypothesis**, rather than an equality forced by a riskless trading package. A higher-yield currency must be expected to depreciate sufficiently under that condition to offset its interest advantage. Expectations are not realized cash flows; replacing a future random conversion with its expectation does not remove risk. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 7]]

**External verification:** Cavallo (2006), “Interest Rates, Carry Trades, and Exchange Rate Movements,” sections “Not profitable in theory, but profitable in practice” and “What is the carry trade?”, distinguishes the parity condition from exchange risk in the actual strategy. This supports the risk qualification; its empirical examples are not additional course assignments. [FRBSF Economic Letter 2006-31](https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2006/11/interest-rates-carry-trades-and-exchange-rate-movements/).


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Currency_Parity_and_Carry_Trade.md#The lecture's peg and non-deliverable-forward example]]; fingerprint `9aaebd51a4ce2a4c8964bbf02d522f5ea81dbc1fbb36583d7990849bc3299c8d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### The lecture's peg and non-deliverable-forward example

The source switches to **Czechoslovak koruna per Deutsche Mark**, $S_{\rm CSK/DEM}$. With $r_{\rm CSK}>r_{\rm DEM}$ the covered forward rate satisfies $F_{\rm CSK/DEM}>S_{\rm CSK/DEM}$. If the future spot rate actually stays at the present peg, selling one DEM forward and buying it spot at maturity earns $F-S_T=F-S_0>0$ koruna. That is the logic behind the lecture's bundled bank trade. The source explicitly mentions fluctuation bands and a peg to a currency basket as practical complications. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 7]]

**Necessary qualification of the source:** slide 7 calls the payoff “risk-free” after replacing future spot by its expectation. A peg or the belief $E_0[S_T]=S_0$ alone does not guarantee $S_T=S_0$. If the peg changes and $S_T>F$, the short DEM forward loses. The source's positive result is conditional on an unchanged executable conversion rate and ignored costs/counterparty constraints. It cannot be generalized into riskless profit merely from a fixed-exchange-rate announcement. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 7]]

**Supplementary definition:** an NDF settles a contractual exchange-rate difference in cash, rather than delivering the underlying currency principal. It is not defined by an interest-differential profit or a peg. This distinguishes the source's particular strategy from the instrument's general definition. See McCauley, Shu and Ma (2014), “Non-deliverable forwards: 2013 and beyond,” opening definition paragraphs, BIS Quarterly Review: [NDF definition](https://www.bis.org/publications/non-deliverable-forwards-2013-and-beyond). Contract-specific settlement currency and fixing must be checked; the course does not supply such terms for this historical example.


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/Currency_Parity_and_Carry_Trade.md#Yen-funded dollar carry trade]]; fingerprint `9aaebd51a4ce2a4c8964bbf02d522f5ea81dbc1fbb36583d7990849bc3299c8d`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Yen-funded dollar carry trade

Slide 8 uses yet another quotation: $S_0$ is **yen per dollar**, and the horizon is one year. Borrow one yen at $r_¥$, convert it into $1/S_0$ dollars and invest at $r_\$$. At maturity the dollar balance is $(1+r_\$)/S_0$. Converting at realized $S_T$ gives $S_T(1+r_\$)/S_0$ yen. Repaying $1+r_¥$ leaves

$$\Pi_T=\frac{S_T}{S_0}(1+r_\$)-(1+r_¥)\quad\text{yen per initial yen borrowed}.$$

Taking expectations gives the slide's expression with $E_0[S_T]$. If the exchange rate stays unchanged, profit is $r_\$-r_¥$. A higher dollar interest rate therefore creates a carry incentive, but yen appreciation means **fewer yen per dollar**, so $S_T$ falls and repayment becomes harder. The strategy breaks even when

$$\frac{S_T}{S_0}=\frac{1+r_¥}{1+r_\$}.$$

Setting expected rather than realized profit to zero gives the corresponding uncovered parity condition. Negative expected exchange movement can offset a positive interest differential; an unexpected stronger movement can produce a loss. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 8]]

**Agent-created illustration from that equation:** at $S_0=100$ yen/dollar, $r_\$=5\%$, $r_¥=1\%$, unchanged spot produces $0.04$ yen per yen borrowed. Break-even is $S_T=100(1.01/1.05)\approx96.19$. If $S_T=90$, profit is $0.9(1.05)-1.01=-0.065$ yen. This is arithmetic under the slide's one-year setup, not a supplied historical result or trading recommendation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Financial_Markets_Instruments_I/Week_3/L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx|L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 8]]

source_units.text:
## Worked example

O017-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. **Prompt:** Borrow one yen for one year at $r_¥=0.01$, convert at $S_0=100\ \mathrm{JPY/USD}$ and invest in dollars at $r_\$=0.05$. No forward covers the dollar conversion. Derive realized yen profit per initial yen, calculate profit at unchanged spot, the break-even spot and profit at $S_T=90$. Contrast a zero expected profit/UIP condition with a guaranteed realized payoff and explain the direction of funding-currency appreciation. Separately a historical-style peg example quotes koruna per DEM: spot peg $20$, short DEM-forward delivery price $21$, and possible terminal spot $23$. Compute profit per DEM if the peg survives and in the latter scenario; explain the source risk-free qualification, bands/basket caveats and what makes a contract an NDF.

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** One initial yen buys $1/S_0$ USD and grows to $(1+r_\$)/S_0$ USD. Converting and repaying leaves $\Pi_T=(S_T/S_0)(1+r_\$)-(1+r_¥)$. Unchanged spot gives $0.04000000$ yen; break-even is $S_T=S_0(1+r_¥)/(1+r_\$)=96.19047619\ \mathrm{JPY/USD}$. At supplied realized spot profit is $-0.06500000$ yen. Yen appreciation means fewer yen per dollar, lowering $S_T$ and harming this yen-funded trade. Setting expected profit to zero replaces $S_T$ by $E_0[S_T]$ but does not guarantee realized profit; UIP is an expectation hypothesis rather than a covered riskless equality. In the koruna-per-DEM example the short forward earns $F-S_T$: unchanged peg gives $1.00000000$ koruna per DEM; supplied changed spot gives $-2.00000000$. A belief or announcement does not force the executable future spot to equal the peg; fluctuation bands, basket movements, costs and counterparty constraints also matter. The source risk-free wording is only conditional on maintained conversion and ignored frictions. An NDF cash-settles a contractual exchange-rate difference instead of delivering principal; it is not defined by a peg, interest differential or guaranteed gain. No missing fixing/settlement terms are invented. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

## Motivation, intuition, and definitions

Price comparable zero coupons, construct the issuing/buying/forward package, derive its forward delivery price and adjacent-period compound yield identity without forecasting future spot yields.
